paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disorder that appears within the first weeks of life. The intestine selectively fails to absorb dietary glucose and galactose. The resulting severe osmotic diarrhea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991; Martín et al., 1996). The disorder is caused by a defect in the intestinal brush border Na+/glucose cotransporter SGLT1 (Martín et al., 1996).

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption results in severe osmotic diarrhea and dehydration.
checks.evidence_quote: The consequent severe diarrhoea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are eliminated from the diet.
checks.explanation: Abstract says severe diarrhoea and dehydration, but does not describe the diarrhoea as 'osmotic'.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) studied glucose transport in vitro by jejunal mucosa from a 3-year-old girl with congenital glucose-galactose malabsorption. Mucosa from 6 normal controls and from her asymptomatic 5-year-old brother accumulated glucose to 16 times the concentration in the incubation medium. The proband's mucosa could not concentrate glucose at any point during a 60-minute incubation. Fructose accumulation was similar in all subjects. Renal glucose titration showed a partial defect in renal glucose reabsorption in the proband. Her unaffected brother had a titration curve similar to those of 7 normal volunteers. The authors concluded that absent intestinal glucose transport is accompanied by partial impairment of renal glucose transport.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) found impaired jejunal glucose transport in both parents and a half sister of a patient with glucose-galactose malabsorption. Their values lay between those of normal controls and the proband. In these heterozygotes, glucose influx was impaired but efflux was normal. Kinetic analysis showed reduced capacity (Vmax) with normal affinity (Km). The authors concluded that the disorder is autosomal recessive and that heterozygotes can be detected. Autosomal recessive inheritance was also supported by the finding of homozygous SLC5A1 mutations in affected members of an Old Order Amish pedigree (Xin and Wang, 2011).

paragraphs.text: Turk et al. (1991) noted that intestinal biopsies from GGM patients show a specific defect in Na(+)-dependent glucose absorption in the brush border. This absorption is normally carried out by the Na+/glucose cotransporter in the brush border membrane of the intestinal epithelium. Turk et al. (1993) stated that SGLT1 is the main carrier protein for intestinal uptake of dietary glucose and galactose. It is a 75-kDa glycoprotein located in the intestinal brush border and is predicted to have 12 membrane spans. SGLT1 couples sugar transport to Na+ gradients across the intestinal brush border, and Martín et al. (1996) concluded that defects in its trafficking and function cause GGM.

paragraphs.text: Martín et al.
